articles.title: Federated Learning: Why Averaging Model Updates Works - and When It Fails
articles.excerpt: Most machine learning still assumes a convenient fiction: all the data sits in one place, ready to be shuffled, split, and trained on. Real data rarely cooperates. It lives on phones, in hospitals, in…
articles.body: Most machine learning still assumes a convenient fiction: all the data sits in one place, ready to be shuffled, split, and trained on. Real data rarely cooperates. It lives on phones, in hospitals, in banks, and in factories, where moving it is expensive, slow, or simply not allowed. Federated learning is the attempt to train anyway, without centralising the data. The core idea is disarmingly simple. Instead of sending data to the model, send the model to the data. Each client trains locally, sends back only an update, and a server averages those updates into a new global model. That averaging step, called Federated Averaging or FedAvg, looks almost too naive to work. Understanding why it usually does work, and exactly where it breaks, is the key to using it well.
articles.author: Umesh Tharuka Malaviarachchi

articles.title: Matter Over Thread vs Tuya ZigBee: What Actually Changes in 2026
articles.excerpt: Matter and ZigBee get compared as if they are the same kind of thing. They are not, and that is why the comparison keeps producing bad advice. ZigBee is both a mesh radio protocol and an application l…
articles.body: Matter and ZigBee get compared as if they are the same kind of thing. They are not, and that is why the comparison keeps producing bad advice. The layer confusion ZigBee is both a mesh radio protocol and an application layer. It defines how devices route packets and it defines what "turn on the light" means. Matter is only an application layer. It says what "turn on the light" means. It does not define a radio for low-power mesh devices. That job goes to Thread, which is a separate IPv6-based mesh protocol that runs on the same 802.15.4 radios as ZigBee. So the real comparison is: Matter over Thread versus the Tuya stack over ZigBee (or over Wi-Fi). And it is a comparison at two different layers, which is why answers like "Matter replaces ZigBee" are wrong in both directions.

articles.title: Adding Tuya Smart Switches to Home Assistant: Three Paths and What Breaks
articles.excerpt: "Tuya" on the box is not one thing. It is a cloud platform, a Wi-Fi firmware stack, and — in the ZigBee range — a ZigBee profile. Which of the three your device actually uses decides what you can do w…
articles.body: "Tuya" on the box is not one thing. It is a cloud platform, a Wi-Fi firmware stack, and — in the ZigBee range — a ZigBee profile. Which of the three your device actually uses decides what you can do with it in Home Assistant, and where the pain is. Path 1: the official cloud integration The Tuya integration talks to the Tuya cloud, not to your device. Your switch reports to Tuya's servers, Home Assistant polls those servers, and a command goes back the same way. The good part: it works with essentially every Tuya device, including ones you will never get local access to. It survives firmware updates, and it works when you are away from home. The bad part: it is polling.

articles.title: EchoLantern: A Private Little Archive for Memories
articles.excerpt: A memory doesn't always arrive as a grand story. Sometimes it's a rattling ceiling fan, a pet waiting at the door, a phrase someone always used, or a small ritual that made an ordinary day feel like h…
articles.body: A memory doesn't always arrive as a grand story. Sometimes it's a rattling ceiling fan, a pet waiting at the door, a phrase someone always used, or a small ritual that made an ordinary day feel like home. I built EchoLantern to give those details a place to stay. What I Built EchoLantern is a local-first keepsake maker for everyday memories, people, places, pets, family stories, and meaningful objects or traditions. A user writes a few rough notes, optionally adds one photo, and creates an editable keepsake card, a short reflective paragraph, a card inscription, and a gentle question for another day. Saved keepsakes live in a searchable archive in the current browser and can be exported as Markdown or JSON.

articles.body: 8 Field Techniques for Smart Contract Auditing — Forged by Refuting My Own Findings I recently spent 24 focused rounds auditing a lending-and-automation codebase for a security competition. I opened 7 attack hypotheses. I closed all 7 — six with proofs, one by refuting my own draft finding at final review, hours before it would have gone to judges as a "Low severity, high confidence" report. That last one hurt, and it taught me more than the six clean refutations. Here are the eight techniques that carried the campaign. Each is small enough to use tomorrow. 1. Rebuild the economic model before reading functions For mechanism contracts (auctions, leases, escrows), don't read top-to-bottom. First reconstruct the economy: who pays whom, when, for what right.

articles.title: CVE-2026-6653 is an SBOM problem before it is a patch problem
articles.excerpt: CVE-2026-6653 is an SBOM problem before it is a patch problem The advisory for CVE-2026-6653 lists libxml2 2.9.11 through versions before 2.11.0 as affected and names 2.11.0 as the fixed release. Read…
articles.body: CVE-2026-6653 is an SBOM problem before it is a patch problem The advisory for CVE-2026-6653 lists libxml2 2.9.11 through versions before 2.11.0 as affected and names 2.11.0 as the fixed release. Reading that as a single package upgrade is the fastest way to leave the vulnerability in production, because most systems do not track libxml2 as a first-class dependency. Where the library hides libxml2 is a C library consumed by language runtimes, document converters, configuration parsers and management appliances. In a containerised estate it can appear three times in one request path: in the base image, in a runtime bundled with an application server, and in a statically linked tool invoked by a batch job. An inventory that queries the package manager only reports the first layer.

articles.title: Analog astronauts: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.excerpt: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.body: I have been dreaming of doing research in space as an astronaut my whole life, but for some reason, the thought of working underwater made me nervous. I’ve known for a long time that astronauts train underwater to simulate different scenarios they’re likely to experience in space. Diving was never an issue for me, either — I even made it as far as becoming a certified rescue diver. So what was the problem? This summer, I led a simulated space mission in an underwater habitat called the Jules’ Undersea Lab. It is a research station that is located 22 feet (6.7 meters) underwater near Key Largo, Florida. You have to scuba dive to get in and out of the station. To become an aquanaut , you have to stay underwater for at least 24 hours in a so-called state of saturation.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 26, 2004: Cassini spacecraft takes 1st-ever closeup photos of Saturn moon Titan
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 26, 2004, NASA's Cassini spacecraft took the first close-up images of Saturn's largest moon Titan. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 26, 2004, NASA's Cassini spacecraft took the first close-up images of Saturn's largest moon Titan. The Cassini spacecraft would later drop off a probe on Titan named Huygens, which was a European spacecraft that hitched a ride to the Saturn system with the Cassini mission. But before Cassini dropped off its robotic passenger, it flew by Titan a few times and took some amazing photos . Cassini completed its first flyby on July 3, 2004, but when it swung by a second time on Oct. 26, it got about 300 times closer than it did the first time. At the closest point of this flyby, Cassini was 745 miles (1,200 kilometers) away from the surface of Titan. The spacecraft took hundreds of photos during this flyby , and these were the highest resolution views of Titan anyone had ever seen.

articles.title: NASA ends Swift space telescope mission after failed rescue attempt
articles.excerpt: NASA has officially ended the mission of its Swift Observatory, after a private satellite failed to meet up with the aging spacecraft in orbit.
articles.body: NASA has officially ended the mission of its Swift space telescope, after a private satellite failed in its bold bid to rescue the aging spacecraft. That rescue mission was led by the Arizona company Katalyst Space Technologies, whose LINK spacecraft tried to meet up with Swift this summer to boost its orbit. That didn't work out, however, so Swift continues its fall back toward Earth. The telescope is expected to reenter Earth's atmosphere "in the next few weeks," NASA said in a statement on Friday (Oct. 23). That statement served primarily to announce the end of the Swift mission after more than 20 very productive years. The telescope launched to Earth orbit in November 2004, tasked with studying gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) — the most powerful explosions in the cosmos.
